newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs investigate protests about EU energy project.
newsitem.headline: MEPs investigate protests about EU energy project.

text.p: Euro-MPs are investigating allegations that the European Commission granted 86 million Ecus to a Northern Ireland-Scotland electricity interconnector which is dangerous and uneconomic.

The European Parliament's energy and budgetary control committees are both examining the project -- one of 10 key trans-European energy network schemes -- after more than 1,000 people in Scotland and Northern Ireland protested to parliament and the Commission.

The protesters say the project between Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) and Scottish Power is potentially dangerous because the undersea section is routed close to Beaufort's Dyke, a deepwater trench in the Irish Sea used by the British government to dump redundant munitions from World War Two.

They say the NIE-Scottish Power contract contravenes EU competition law and a forthcoming EU electricity directive because it commits NIE to taking an annual 1,250 gigawatt hours of electricity for the next 15 years and restricts third party access to the link.

The contract also gives NIE, a privatised company with a natural monopoly over transmission and distribution in Northern Ireland, a foothold in the generation market, despite the decision at privatisation two years ago to separate generation and supply to encourage competition, they say.
The Commission's directorate-general for regional policy (DGXVI) was unavailable for comment on Thursday.

Struan Stevenson, a consultant acting on behalf of the petitioners and a British Conservative MP, told Reuters the laying of a Scotland-Northern Ireland gas interconnector through the Beaufort Dyke area last year dislodged 7,000 incendiary devices which were washed up on local beaches.
An imminent British government seabed survey is expected to say this month that laying the electricity cable will cause far less disturbance, Stevenson said.
But it may also recommend the complete re-mapping of the dump site before a decision is taken on the route of the interconnector.

"We want a public inquiry for environmental and safety checks," he said. "The applicants for the project published a skimpy environmental impact assessment (EIA) on the undersea area and gave scant reference to Beaufort."

Dutch Socialist Euro-MP Pieter Dankert has asked the Commission to say why there was no independent, comprehensive EIA and whether conducting one would alter the project's initial cost-benefit analysis.
On behalf of parliament's budgetary control committee, Dankert is also asking the Commission to address the petitioners' concerns about the project's economic aspects.
Parliament's energy committee is also due to raise this issue in December.
Both committees want the Commission to give further justification for granting 86 million Ecus from the European Regional Development Fund to the project.

According to energy committee rapporteur Nuala Ahern, the Commission argued in favour of the grant in 1993 on the grounds that the interconnector would meet generating capacity deficits in Northern Ireland and do away with the isolated nature of the province's electricity system.
The grant was made conditional on the authorities undertaking to cut electricity prices and carry out an EIA.
"I will tell the energy committee we should revaluate Northern Ireland's electricity requirements and look at the (NIE-Scottish Power) contract," Ahern, an Irish Green MEP, told Reuters said.

Since the 250 megawatt project was approved four years ago, the gas interconnector has been built and the Ireland-Northern Ireland electricity interconnector has been reopened, reducing its power deficit and its isolation, she said.
NIE's 15-year contract with Scottish Power would swamp the system and reduce the ability of local generators to compete for a share of the market.

The cost of bringing in power through the expensive marine interconnection could also be passed on to consumers in Northern Ireland, who already pay more for their electricity than any other part of the United Kingdom, she added.

Dankert has asked the Commission to say whether the NIE- Scottish Power contract should be reviewed in the light of an expected Monopolies and Mergers Commission inquiry into Northern Ireland's electricity generation industry.
